content:
Trellis has formalized the Strong Perfect Graph Theorem of Maria Chudnovsky, Neil Robertson, Paul Seymour, Robin Thomas.

It was an autonomous run of around 6 weeks, resulting in around 540,000 lines of lean code (all used for the main theorem).

Original paper here:
https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2006/164-1/p02

Github here:
https://github.com/wpegden/spgt

A nice viewer to browse the formalization is available here:
https://www.math.cmu.edu/~wes/trellis.php

I believe this is the largest single-theorem lean proof by quite some margin (that is public, at least). I had an agent do a size analysis at the end, this is included as-is in the repo (e.g., it found around 10% of the code lies in blocks of duplicated lines).

How much did it cost? I understand from your formalization.yaml file that you're using gpt-5.6-sol xhigh for everything, via subscriptions, but how many subscriptions did you need? One $20 subscription? 100 $200 subscriptions?

This was one chatgpt pro ($200) subscription for the 6 weeks. I would say it was usually using about 80% of the budget.

Cost at API rates look enormous, I include an table of token usage below. One thing to note is that the vast majority of token usage - and roughly half the cost at API billing rates - is actually just cached tokens.

input tokens 12,983.4 M (12.98 B)
cached 12,279.4 M 94.6%
fresh 704.0 M
output tokens 69.9 M
reasoning 31.5 M 45.1%

So, subscription cost: ~$300
API-equivalent cost $11,756.87

Thanks! I'm surprised that the formalization.yaml file didn't have a place for these figures -- or did you not want to put them there for some reason? It's a very cool result! Will you do the graph minor theorem next?
Good point, I will add them. GMT would be a great target; maybe not "next" though!
Is the original sequence of papers by Robertson and Seymour still the only complete proof of the Graph Minor Theorem?

Right, if I was going to do this, I would start by having AI prepare in natural language a modern version of the proof that is complete end to end but includes the simplifications that came later. I don't think this already exists.
